rationale: X matches the references by delivering a comprehensive, implementation-neutral shaping brief that covers the requested actors, constraints, baseline behavior, desired outcomes, examples, compatibility risks, open questions, and external success signals. Its account of argument shifting, URL conversion, verb inference, CSRF token handling, form-versus-control attributes, block capture, remote and disabled options, and legacy button generation agrees with the checkout's helper source and navigation-helper tests. It also distinguishes observed behavior from hypotheses and avoids prescribing markup, new options, JavaScript behavior, internal changes, or test implementation.

shortcomings.summary: Two requested baseline edges remain hypotheses.
shortcomings.evidence: X leaves nil-destination behavior and unsafe string-label escaping unresolved because dedicated button_to tests are absent, even though focused source tracing or execution could have established the current behavior more decisively; the references make the same conservative limitation, so this does not make X materially worse.

strengths.evidence: X correctly covers string and block forms, default POST, GET, DELETE and inferred PATCH, authenticity-token variants, nested form attributes, remote and disabled behavior, false destinations, missing labels, and the legacy input-versus-button setting.

strengths.summary: All requested user-facing cases are made reviewable.
strengths.evidence: The brief supplies concrete examples and desired outcomes for string labels, blocks, GET, POST, DELETE, remote forms, disabled controls, nested form options, explicit tokens, nil URLs, and unsafe HTML labels, then identifies compatibility risks and open decisions.

X frames accessibility and predictability as externally observable outcomes, labels unverified claims, states discovery limits, and explicitly avoids prescribing markup, options, JavaScript behavior, internal helper design, or test implementation.
